turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Arthur? Come through. I took your observations in the waiting room so we're not starting from scratch.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I'm tired, and I'd like this over with.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure was one fifty-two over ninety... no, I've misread my figures, it's one forty-six over eighty-four. Pulse seventy-six. Oxygen ninety-seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thank you. He's been very short with me all morning.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not short. I'm just sat here.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Arthur, Jean, I'm Dr Shah. Sorry, the clinic's overrun.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I made this appointment. He wasn't keen.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Because I'm fine. This is a waste of time.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Jean, um, what are you actually seeing at home? Arthur, I'll want your version straight after, even where it clashes.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He repeats questions. What day is it, have we had lunch, where the paper is. Five minutes on, he asks the same again.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not repeat myself. You don't listen, that's all.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you don't agree on that. Jean, from your point of view, how long has the repeating been going on?
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): A year. Easily a year.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): It isn't a year, and it isn't happening. Well, actually, if anything it'd be a couple of months, which it isn't.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll park the timing, given you don't agree it's even going on. Anything else, Jean?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He forgets appointments. Missed the dentist last month, and the chiropodist the month before that. They're on the calendar. He still doesn't go.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't forget. I knew about both. I didn't fancy going. The dentist is rough.

[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Then there was him getting lost. He went to the corner shop for a paper and some milk, ten minutes usually, and he was gone nearly two hours. A neighbour found him two streets away, and he couldn't say which way was home.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not lost. I fancied a walk. I knew precisely where I was.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): And when was this?
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Um, I keep saying Tuesday, but it might have been the week before. I can't pin the day down.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Doesn't matter, she's got it wrong.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Finding words? Names for ordinary things?
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh yes. Kettle, the remote, even our dog, and we've had him nine years. That's been about three months.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog's called Buster, thank you. Words do stick, I'll admit that. But it's not three months. More like eight.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both of you notice words sticking, then. Three months versus eight. I'll note roughly three to eight months, rather than pretend we've got a start date.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he left the gas hob on last week. I came in to the smell, empty pan, ring still lit.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That was once. I was going back to turn it off. Don't make a production of it.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Once still matters to me. Have you had any falls?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't fall.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No falls. He's steady on his feet.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Any weakness down one side, or fits?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Nothing like that. I'm tired, that's the whole of it.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tired how, exactly?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Worn out. Today, and most days, if you want the truth. I nod off in the chair after lunch.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Every afternoon, an hour, sometimes two. We live in the bungalow together and I'm there all day, so I see it.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or getting breathless when you walk?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I walk fine. The knees ache, but that's years old.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): The knees, yes. What have you been told about them?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Arthritis, at the hospital. I take paracetamol when they play up.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two tablets... or three, I'm not certain which, he decides on the day. Not every day.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the rest of the medicines? Computer's crawling, I haven't the repeat list.

[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do all of them. He doesn't touch the boxes. Ramipril each morning, five milligrams... no, sorry, five was the old dose. It's ten milligrams now, one every morning, for his blood pressure.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm perfectly able to sort my own tablets.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You're not, love. Last month I found three of the night ones still in the packet.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Which night ones are those?
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The atorvastatin. Forty milligrams, one at night, for the cholesterol. Well, I'm fairly sure on the forty.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): It's twenty. I've seen the packet. Not forty.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the dose is not settled, which is awkward. Is he actually swallowing that night one?
[SEG0050] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I put it out. Some mornings it's still there. I couldn't tell you he's taking it properly.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): I take what she puts out. Mostly.
[SEG0052] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There's also a yellow capsule for the leg cramps at night. Different bottle entirely. The name won't come to me.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): People are often given quinine for cramps. Is that familiar?
[SEG0054] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It might be quinine. Um, I won't swear to it. He takes one at bedtime.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Horrible bitter thing. Yes, I do take it.
[SEG0056] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I did buy some biotin, only because my sister takes it for her hair and her nails. He has not had any. That's her thing, not a tablet of his.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): And I don't want it.

[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While we're listing tablets, I'm on metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day, for my diabetes. That's me, not him. His brother Derek, though, had a stroke around sixty.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Did either of his parents have dementia, or memory trouble?
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Not that I know of. His mother was sharp right up to ninety.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): And since she'll mention the job, I drove buses for thirty years. Retired at sixty-five. I have not forgotten the roads.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): That picture helps, oddly. I'm going to listen to your chest and look at your ankles.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, the pulse is regular, no ankle swelling. You know it's Thursday and that you're at the surgery, so you're orientated today.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): The blood pressure is ongoing, we know that, and the cholesterol as well. Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataracts, both eyes, years ago. That's the lot.
[SEG0066] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Right eye twice, left eye once. The last one was about eight years ago.

[SEG0067] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to give this a name today, it wouldn't be honest after one chat. What I'm thinking is we do bloods, a full count, kidneys, thyroid, B12, folate and a glucose, to look for things we can actually put right. And I'll arrange a proper memory assessment rather than rush some score in this room.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want a memory test. I've told you I'm fine.

[SEG0069] person_4 (DOCTOR): I've heard you, and I'm still arranging both. Don't go to the shops alone for now, and don't light the hob unless Jean is in the kitchen. Leave the tablets to her, and bring the statin box when you come back and see me in about three weeks, after the bloods. Nurse will sort the forms on your way out.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

omissions.text: No known allergy information was discussed or recorded; no omission.
Caregiver additionally stated he is steady on his feet when falls were discussed.

Patient explicitly denied only repeating himself and getting lost, but also said words 'do stick' / word-finding trouble is present; this supports the symptom being acknowledged by the patient as well as the caregiver, not just reported_by caregiver.
Patient said he is tired 'today, and most days' and that this is essentially his only symptom ('I'm tired, that's the whole of it'). The emphasis that tiredness is the main complaint is not captured.

Medication adherence concern extends beyond general medicine management: caregiver said he 'doesn't touch the boxes' and that she found three of the night tablets still in the packet last month before clarifying these were atorvastatin.

Possible quinine for leg cramps was suggested by the doctor and accepted only tentatively by the caregiver; patient then confirmed he does take the bitter bedtime capsule. The current record names it only as an unnamed yellow capsule and misses the patient's confirmation of use.
Caregiver's metformin 500 mg twice daily for diabetes was explicitly stated to be her medication, not the patient's; this distinction is clinically important if any system might attribute it to him.
Doctor specifically said he was not going to 'rush some score in this room' and instead would arrange a proper memory assessment, reflecting that no bedside cognitive score was performed today.

Patient objected to memory testing ('I don't want a memory test. I've told you I'm fine'), and the doctor explicitly stated he had heard him but was still arranging both bloods and memory assessment. This disagreement about the plan is not recorded.
Doctor said the nurse would sort the blood forms on the way out.
